name: Alice, Bob and Chocolate
title: Alice, Bob and Chocolate
problem_statement: Alice and Bob like games. And now they are ready to start a new game. They have placed n chocolate bars in a line. Alice starts to eat chocolate bars one by one from left to right, and Bob — from right to left. For each chocolate bar the time, needed for the player to consume it, is known (Alice and Bob eat them with equal speed). When the player consumes a chocolate bar, he immediately starts with another. It is not allowed to eat two chocolate bars at the same time, to leave the bar unfinished and to make pauses. If both players start to eat the same bar simultaneously, Bob leaves it to Alice as a true gentleman. How many bars each of the players will consume?
input_format: The first line contains one integer n (1≤n≤10^5) — the amount of bars on the table. The second line contains a sequence t1, t2, ..., tn (1 ≤ ti ≤ 1000), where ti is the time (in seconds) needed to consume the i-th bar (in the order from left to right).
output_format: Print two numbers a and b, where a is the amount of bars consumed by Alice, and b is the amount of bars consumed by Bob.

examples.title: Minimum size n=1, Alice takes all
examples.why_included: Tests the absolute minimum input size. Alice always gets the single bar, regardless of its eating time.

examples.title: Problem statement example case
examples.why_included: This is the example provided in the problem statement, essential for verifying basic logic.

examples.title: Two bars, Alice is faster
examples.why_included: Tests a small case where Alice finishes quickly, allowing Bob to start his bar sooner, resulting in a tie.

examples.title: Two bars, Bob is faster
examples.why_included: Symmetrical case to the previous one. Alice takes her bar, Bob takes his. The times affect who starts next, but with only two bars, the outcome is the same.

examples.title: Two bars, equal time
examples.why_included: Tests the case with two bars of equal time. Alice and Bob each take one.

examples.title: All bars have equal time, odd n
examples.why_included: When all times are equal, Alice gets the extra bar due to the 'gentleman' rule (or the tie-break going to the person with less time).

examples.title: All bars have equal time, even n
examples.why_included: With an even number of equal-time bars, they should split them evenly.

examples.title: Alice is much faster and takes all
examples.why_included: Tests a scenario where Alice's bars are much faster, allowing her to eat more before Bob can finish his first one.

examples.title: Bob is much faster and takes more
examples.why_included: The reverse of the previous case. Bob gets many fast bars while Alice is stuck on a slow one.

examples.title: Symmetrical times, odd n
examples.why_included: Tests a symmetrical array. Alice gets the middle bar because she and Bob finish their outer bars at the same cumulative time.

examples.title: Symmetrical times, even n
examples.why_included: Tests a symmetrical array with even length. The bars should be split evenly.

examples.title: Alice gets one huge bar, Bob gets many small
examples.why_included: A classic adversarial case where one player takes a single time-consuming task, allowing the other player to complete many small tasks in the meantime.

examples.title: Bob gets one huge bar, Alice gets many small
examples.why_included: The reverse of the previous adversarial case, ensuring the logic is symmetrical.

examples.title: Perfectly balanced split
examples.why_included: Tests a case where the total time of the first half equals the total time of the second half. The split should be exactly in the middle.

examples.title: Almost balanced, Alice gets one more
examples.why_included: Similar to the balanced case, but with an extra small bar in the middle that Alice claims due to the tie-break rule.

examples.title: Sorted ascending times
examples.why_included: Alice gets slow bars and Bob gets fast ones, so Bob is expected to eat more.

examples.title: Sorted descending times
examples.why_included: The reverse of the sorted case. Alice gets fast bars and is expected to eat more.

examples.title: Alternating small and large times
examples.why_included: Tests the back-and-forth nature of the simulation. One player gets ahead, then the other catches up.

examples.title: All times are minimum value 1
examples.why_included: A specific instance of the 'all-equal' case using the minimum possible time value.

examples.title: All times are maximum value 1000
examples.why_included: A specific instance of the 'all-equal' case using the maximum possible time value.

examples.title: Small random case
examples.why_included: A small, arbitrary test case to catch any weird interactions. Seed: 42.

examples.title: Medium random case
examples.why_included: A medium-sized random case to ensure the logic holds for non-trivial lengths. Seed: 123.

examples.title: Maximum n, all times 1
examples.why_included: Stress test with maximum n and minimum times. The even split is expected.

examples.title: Maximum n-1, all times 1
examples.why_included: Stress test with near-maximum n (odd). Alice should get the extra one.

examples.title: Maximum n, all times 1000
examples.why_included: Stress test with maximum n and maximum times. Checks for potential overflow, though not an issue with standard 64-bit integers.

examples.title: Maximum n, random times
examples.why_included: This is effectively an 'all-equal' case with max N, but presented as random to ensure the logic doesn't fail on specific repeated values. Seed: 7.

examples.title: Maximum n, alternating 1 and 1000
examples.why_included: A stress test with a pathological pattern that forces the lead to switch back and forth constantly. This tests the core loop logic under high iterations.

examples.title: Maximum n, sorted ascending
examples.why_included: Stress test where Bob is heavily favored. The distribution should be skewed heavily towards Bob.

examples.title: Maximum n, sorted descending, Alice favored
examples.why_included: Stress test where Alice is heavily favored due to getting all the fast bars first. This checks the two-pointer logic at scale under a strong bias.

examples.title: Large central bar surrounded by small bars
examples.why_included: Tests the tie-breaking rule after both players have accumulated equal time. The large central bar is a red herring; the outcome depends on the symmetrical wings.

examples.title: Alice takes one very slow bar initially
examples.why_included: An extreme case where one player is stuck, allowing the other to consume nearly all remaining items. This verifies the core greedy choice mechanism.

examples.title: Bob takes one very slow bar initially
examples.why_included: Symmetrical to the previous case, ensures the logic is not biased towards one player. Alice gets to consume almost everything.

examples.title: Leapfrogging accumulated times with alternating values
examples.why_included: This case tests the simulation's correctness when the player with less accumulated time frequently changes, ensuring the greedy choice is made correctly at each step.

examples.title: Multiple perfect ties on accumulated time
examples.why_included: Tests the tie-breaking condition (`<=`) multiple times mid-game, not just at the end. Correct handling is crucial for this case.

examples.title: Large random case near maximum N
examples.why_included: A general stress test with large, pseudo-random data to verify performance and correctness on typical large inputs. Seed: 1337.

examples.title: Palindromic sequence of chocolate times
examples.why_included: Tests a perfectly symmetrical input. The logic should consistently break ties in Alice's favor, leading her to claim the central bar.
